Okay. We'll leave that. I want to get back to some technical stuff. You mentioned EQ, which is equalization. Right. Maybe you could. On your first. Well. On the first board you had in that first J&M.

Nothing. Nothing.

Explain equalization.
Okay. Well.
What that means.
There are a couple of major areas where equalization is used.
Okay.

One is in the mid to upper range to increase or decrease presence or brightness. In the low mid range you increase presence. 2,500K, 2K, 3K, 1,000 Hertz. Right. Okay. Okay. In the upper, you know, from 5, 7, up like that, the brightness. Okay. So if you could increase that, you would increase it like symbols. If you bumped 5 or 7K up a little bit or these days 10K maybe, you'd get symbols brighter and more incisive, cutting more and more sizzle. Yeah. After.
Yeah.

A voice, if you bumped up 2,500, 3,000, you know, 2.53K, you get more presence. If you bump up the low end, and there again, you might get more balls. Right. More that low end full sound. That's so good. And at the very low end, you can roll off a lot of low frequency garbage that's bouncing around that's just muddying up the recording. Yeah. Unfortunately, to do that, you need a filter rather than an equalizer. A filter is like an equalizer except the curves of the response are much sharper. In other words, if a filter would say whack everything from 40 Hertz down out pretty good, where an equalizer would just taper it off so you'd still have something of the harmonic below it, say 20 Hertz, you'd still have a fair amount of 20 when you're affecting 40 with an equalizer. But with a filter, you could take 40 down a couple of dB and have 20 almost gone.
Mm-hmm.
That kind of, because the curve, the response curve is much sharper.
And... But on those early records, you had... I had none of that.

None of that. Absolutely nothing. And then, like I say, through this digging into the motion picture thing, I got a hold of... There was a company called Cinema that used Western Electric and IRPE patents and built equalizers for the motion picture industry.
Mm-hmm.

And the motion picture industry used equalizers like this, presence, which would be 3 and 5K, boost or dip. If somebody had a tinny sounding voice, you could actually dip that a little bit and make them maybe sound more rounded. Low end for generally music, not voices. Very few people, you want to boost the low end. And there was a way to do that, incidentally, without EQ, and I did that before I had EQ, is that the ribbon microphones are a velocity microphone.
Mm-hmm.
They detect the velocity of the air particles. That's because they... That's why you have the ribbon. That's right. Yeah, the ribbon does that. Yeah. It's very light ribbon being flooded by the...
But it's very sensitive as well.

Yeah, right. Well, since they have a velocity microphone, if you got up close to it, it would accentuate the low end. So... And the old-time radio operators used to do it. They'd get right up close to a microphone and don't talk right into it because it would
pop, you know? Mm-hmm. And they'd get that big...

Deep voice, right. ...old-time radio announcer sound. Right. Yeah. And I found out about that. So I used it by getting vocalists to be up close if they needed some low-end bump or that kind of thing. Mm-hmm. And then, like I said, I got ahold of a couple of cinema equalizers and a filter. Mm-hmm. And that helped things. But then I could only use it after the mix. Or what I finally did was buy a separate microphone preamp for the vocalist so I could use it because I'd have to bring it up to line level to use these. These were line level things. Mm-hmm. They couldn't use them on microphones the way consoles do, you know, single microphone input. You could take that one microphone and do things. Well, so I had this one microphone preamp for the vocalist. And I could run... Then I got up line level. So I could do things with the equalizers and filters on the vocal. Again, minimally. These filters are very good for the quality of them. Filters and equalizers also introduce phase shift. Mm-hmm. So you have to be careful there, too.

And that's painful.

Mm-hmm.
But he drove a hard bargain. He was a miserly guy to work out a contract with. Mm-hmm. And he didn't mind if you were in a bind, taking advantage of that bind.
Mm-hmm.

I mean...

To King.
